title: Token origin linkage study & heuristic matrix (scratch)
content:
Purpose: quick research notes and an actionable signal matrix to map observed token/credential floods to likely origin profiles and tuned mitigations. This is a scratchpad for oncall + SRE experiments — not final runbook text.

High-level summary (short):
- We observed a multi-phase traffic flood on 2025-11-10 that produced ~3.6M requests over 6 hours to the inference API, with ~68% of requests using a small set (~920) of API keys.
- Traffic morphology is heterogeneous: a volumetric flood (high qps short spikes), followed by a sustained low-latency drip with polyglot User-Agent strings and repeating prompt templates.
- Primary hypothesis: a credential scraping + reuse campaign that combines automated rotation of header fingerprints with opportunistic payload templating.

Why this is different from prior events:
- Key reuse across regions and product routes (hosted embeddings + chat endpoints) in parallel — suggests a distributed reuse botnet or a lateral credential leak across multiple customers.
- Requests show deliberate pacing (exponential backoff-like inter-request distribution) and engineered token caching attempts (prefix replays).

Immediate goals for this note:
- Define an explainable "signal matrix" that maps metrics to likely origin classes (credential leakage vs. scripted origin vs. proxy-rotated botnet).
- Document quick mitigations we can reasonably apply while preserving legitimate traffic and minimizing false positives.
- Outline testable telemetry queries and a short experiment plan for tuned rate limits / WAF signatures.

Observed signals (raw):
- Distinct token clusters: 920 keys accounted for 68% of flood traffic. Top 10 keys each produced 40k–220k requests during the storm window.
- UA churn: ~14k distinct User-Agent strings; many are short-lived and contain odd truncations (e.g., "curl/7.8x", "python-requests/2.2.1rc1").
- IP distribution: 12k unique IPv4s, but with heavy concentration in certain ASNs (ASN 39520, ASN 6939).
- Geo spread: requests originate from 28 countries with bursts synchronized to UTC-aligned minutes (sharp 1–2 minute spikes).
- Prompt similarity: 82% of requests used one of 6 prompt templates; many include identical top-of-prompt prefixes (candidate for prefix caching).
- KV-cache probing: repeated short continuation requests that request short completions but repeatedly specify the same context window id; likely attempting to prime or reuse server-side caching.

Signal matrix (simple):
- Signature A (credential scrape + reuse): key reuse across regions + prompt template reuse + rapid UA churn + low request jitter per key.
- Signature B (rotating proxy botnet): high IP diversity + UA churn + per-key low volume + asynchronous region-only spikes.
- Signature C (single script gone wild): small IP set + stable UA + high per-key qps + linear increase in throughput.

Mapping rules (heuristic):
- If key_cluster_size < 200 AND median_qps_per_key > 50 => likely C (script).
- If unique_ips_per_key > 40 AND ip_asn_entropy high => likely B (proxy botnet).
- If same_key_seen_across_regions AND prompt_template_entropy low => likely A (credential reuse).
- These are intentionally permissive; use as triage labels, not enforcement gates.

Quick mitigation recipes (oncall friendly):
1) Soft cooldown (recommended first-line):
   - Apply a per-key temporary soft-slowdown: lower rate limit window from 100r/s to 10r/s for keys matching "top-1000 flood list" for 30m.
   - Command (internal): /tools/qcontrol apply --keys-file /tmp/top-flood-keys.csv --rate 10rps --window 30m --reason "investigation-cooldown"
   - Rationale: preserves ability for legitimate clients to continue at low rate while reducing cost and blast radius.

2) Region-scoped isolation:
   - If same key observed in multiple regions concurrently, temporarily pin key to original region of last-known-good usage and reject cross-region calls with 409 + structured error to encourage client migration.
   - Implementation note: requires routing table toggle (feature flag: region-pin-v1).

3) WAF quick signatures (only after validation):
   - Create signature to target UA patterns that are synthetic (regex list) and high reuse IP ranges tied to ASN anomalies. Add to "monitor" mode for 2h, escalate to "block" if FP rate < 2%.
   - Example regex: ^(curl|python-requests|node-fetch|Go-http-client|Wget)

4) Prefix reuse detection + cheap challenge:
   - If same request prefix (first 128 chars) seen > N times from different IPs but same key, inject a cheap challenge header requirement (e.g., require X-Client-Nonce for next 5 requests) to raise cost for stateless reuse.

Telemetry queries to run (examples):
- BigQuery-ish pseudo: SELECT key, COUNT(*) as reqs, APPROX_QUANTILES(req_latency_ms,5) FROM requests WHERE ts BETWEEN '2025-11-10T02:00' AND '2025-11-10T10:00' GROUP BY key ORDER BY reqs DESC LIMIT 1000;
- IP-ASN mapping: SELECT ip, asn, COUNT(*) FROM requests WHERE key IN (top-keys) GROUP BY ip, asn ORDER BY COUNT DESC LIMIT 20000;
- Prompt-template clustering: run lightweight simhash on first 200 chars and group; COUNT(*) per cluster to find dominant templates.

Experiment plan (3 steps):
- Phase 0 (30m): apply soft cooldown to top-1000 keys; monitor system-level latency and 95th percentile token cost.
- Phase 1 (2h): enable UA-monitor WAF signatures in "alert" mode + geo pin for keys crossing regions. Measure FP by sampling 500 requests per minute and manual review.
- Phase 2 (24h): roll out prefix-challenge to keys that survive Phase 1 and show cross-IP prefix reuse.

Failure modes & notes:
- False positive risk: enterprise clients behind large NATs or CDNs may show high IP diversity. Always cross-reference customer support tickets and recent deploys (linked artifact: INF-2142).
- Billing/backblast: soft cooldown keeps billing lower but could break high-volume, legitimate batch jobs; include a support escalation flow to lift limits fast.
- Telemetry lag: our observability pipeline currently has ~60s ingestion lag; faster oncall decisions require pushing high-signal metrics to the urgent channel.

Owner escalation & playbook snippets (for oncall):
- Primary: Avery Chen (SRE) — owns triage and initial soft cooldown.
- Secondary: Jordan Patel (Infra) — owns region pin toggles and routing flags.
- If keys belong to named customers and cross-region pinning is applied, loop in CSM and Solutions Eng (runbook step: send templated email + investigative summary).

Follow-ups / open experiments:
- Build a small ML classifier (lightweight) to predict origin class using features: (requests_per_key, unique_ips_per_key, prompt_template_entropy, median_inter_request_gap). Prototype on 2025-11-10 window; target 0.85 precision for class B detection.
- Add an internal dashboard: "key-geometry" chart showing unique_ip_count vs median_qps for top-500 keys.
- Evaluate cost-benefit of prefix-challenge vs per-key cooldown (run small AB test with 10 keys each).

Quick checklist for next oncall shift:
- [ ] Run top-key query and dump to /tmp/top-flood-keys.csv
- [ ] Apply soft cooldown (command above) if still active
- [ ] Enable UA-monitor WAF list in alert mode
- [ ] Snapshot a 10k-sample for manual prompt-template review and paste into #sre-abuse for hand-review

Notes-to-self:
- Keep mitigations reversible and visible in alert timelines.
- Avoid global hard blocks without cross-team signoff.
- Capture customer-facing blurb template for support once a key is pinned or cooled.

Attachments to prepare after investigation (post-incident):
- CSV: key, first_seen_ts, last_seen_ts, total_reqs, unique_ips, top_prompt_template
- Heatmap: per-region per-minute qps for top-50 keys
- Short timeline: list of actions taken + rollback timestamps + measurable impact on cost and latency

References:
- INF-2142 (investigation ticket), PR traffic-tools/#78 (scripts used for sampling), earlier SRE notes on credential floods (see internal Confluence link above).

End of scratchpad.

-- Avery
